e-14805.problem: Find the least common multiple of $4(x+1)$ and $6(x+1).$
e-14805.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\textrm{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

First, we find $\textrm{LCM}(4,6)\mathbin{:}$

- Multiples of $4\mathbin{:}$ $\quad 4, \, 8, \, {\color{blue}12}, \ldots$

- Multiples of $6\mathbin{:}$ $\quad 6, \, {\color{blue}12}, \, 18, \ldots$

So, $\textrm{LCM}(4,6) =  {\color{blue}{12}}.$

Since the variable part is the same in the expressions, we have

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left((x+1), \, (x+1)\right) = {\color{red}{(x+1)}}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left(4(x+1), \, 6(x+1)\right) = {\color{blue}{12}}\cdot {\color{red}{(x+1)}} = 12(x+1).
$$

e-14809.problem: Find the least common multiple of $9(x-1)^4$ and $12(x-1)^2.$
e-14809.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\textrm{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

First, we find $\textrm{LCM}(9,12)\mathbin{:}$

- Multiples of $9 \mathbin{:}$ $\quad 9, \, 18, \, 27, \, {\color{blue}36}, \, 45, \ldots$

- Multiples of $12 \mathbin{:}$ $\quad 12, \, 24, \, {\color{blue}36}, \, 48, \ldots$

So, $\textrm{LCM}(9,12) =  {\color{blue}{36}}.$

To find the $\textrm{LCM}$ of $(x-1)^4$ and $(x-1)^2,$ we raise $(x-1)$ to the largest power that appears in the expressions, which is $4.$ Therefore,

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left((x-1)^4, \, (x-1)^2\right) = {\color{red}{(x-1)^4}}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left(9(x-1)^4, \, 12(x-1)^2\right) = {\color{blue}{36}}\cdot {\color{red}{(x-1)^4}} = 36(x-1)^4.
$$

e-14813.knowledge_point: Finding the LCM of Two Multivariable Polynomials
e-14813.problem: Find the least common multiple of the polynomials $6(x+3)^2(y+1)^2$ and $9(x+3)(y+1)^4.$
e-14813.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\textrm{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

First, we find $\textrm{LCM}(6,9)\mathbin{:}$

- Multiples of $6\mathbin{:}$ $\quad 6, \, 12, \, {\color{blue}18}, \, 24, \ldots$

- Multiples of $9\mathbin{:}$ $\quad 9, \, {\color{blue}18}, \, 27, \ldots$

So, $\textrm{LCM}(6,9) =  {\color{blue}{18}}.$

To find the $\textrm{LCM}$ of $(x+3)^2(y+1)^2$ and $(x+3)(y+1)^4,$ we find the largest powers for $(x+3)$ and $(y+1)$ that appear in the expressions:

- For $(x+3)^2$ and $(x+3),$ the largest power is ${\color{blue}{2}}.$

- For $(y+1)^2$ and $(y+1)^4,$ the largest power is ${\color{red}{4}}.$

Now, we raise $(x+3)$ and $(y+1)$ to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left((x+3)^2(y+1)^2, \,(x+3)(y+1)^4\right) =(x+3)^{\color{blue}{2}}\cdot (y+1)^{\color{red}{4}}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left(6(x+3)^2(y+1)^2, \, 9(x+3)(y+1)^4\right) = 18(x+3)^2 (y+1)^4.
$$

e-14815.knowledge_point: Finding the LCM of Three Polynomials
e-14815.problem: Find the least common multiple of the polynomials $12(x+2)^4 (y+1),$ $\,9(x+2) (y+1)^2,$ and $6(x+2)^2 (y+1)^3.$
e-14815.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\textrm{LCM}$) of three polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

First, we find $\textrm{LCM}(12, 9, 6)\mathbin{:}$

- Multiples of $12\mathbin{:}$ $\quad 12, \, 24, \, {\color{blue}36}, \, 48, \ldots$

- Multiples of $9\mathbin{:}$ $\quad 9, \, 18, \, 27, \, {\color{blue}36}, \, 45, \ldots$

- Multiples of $6 \mathbin{:}$ $\quad 6, \, 12, \, 18, \, 24, \, 30, \, {\color{blue}36}, \ldots$

So, $\textrm{LCM}(12, 9, 6) =  {\color{blue}{36}}.$

To find the $\textrm{LCM}$ of $(x+2)^4 (y+1), (x+2) (y+1)^2,$ and $(x+2)^2 (y+1)^3,$ we find the largest powers for $(x+2)$ and $(y+1)$ that appear in all these expressions:

- For $(x+2)^4,(x+2),$ and $(x+2)^2,$ the largest power is ${\color{blue}{4}}.$

- For $(y+1),(y+1)^2,$ and $(y+1)^3,$ the largest power is ${\color{red}{3}}.$

Now, we raise $(x+2)$ and $(y+1)$ to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

$$
\textrm{LCM}\left((x+2)^4 (y+1), \,(x+2) (y+1)^2,\,(x+2)^2 (y+1)^3\right) =(x+2)^{\color{blue}{4}}\cdot (y+1)^{\color{red}{3}}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \text{LCM}(12(x+2)^{4}(y+1),\,9(x+2)(y+1)^{2},\,6(x+2)^{2}(y+1)^{3}) \\  & =36\cdot (x+2)^{4}\cdot (y+1)^{3} \\  & =36(x+2)^{4}(y+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the least common multiple (LCM) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find LCM(10,15):

  • Multiples of 10: 10,20,30,40,…

  • Multiples of 15: 15,30,45,…

So, LCM(10,15)=30.

Since the variable part is the same in the expressions, we have LCM((y+1),(y+1))=(y+1).

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

LCM(10(y+1),15(y+1))=30⋅(y+1)=30(y+1).

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the least common multiple of $2(z-4)^{2}$ and $7(z-4)^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(2,7):$

- Multiples of $2:$ $\,2,\,4,…,\,12,\,14,16,…$

- Multiples of $7:$ $\,7,\,14,\,21,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(2,7)=14.$

Since the variable part is the same in the expressions, we have

$$
\text{LCM}((z-4)^{2},\,(z-4)^{2})=(z-4)^{2}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\text{LCM}(2(z-4)^{2},\,7(z-4)^{2})=14\cdot (z-4)^{2}=14(z-4)^{2}.
$$

- Multiples of $10:$ $\,10,\,20,\,30,\,40,\,50,…$

Since the variable part is the same in the expressions, we have

$$
\text{LCM}((z-1)^{2},\,(z-1)^{2})=(z-1)^{2}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\text{LCM}(4(z-1)^{2},\,10(z-1)^{2})=20\cdot (z-1)^{2}=20(z-1)^{2}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Find the least common multiple of $10(y+1)^{6}$ and $15(y+1)^{4}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(10,15):$

- Multiples of $10:$ $\,10,\,20,\,30,\,40,…$

- Multiples of $15:$ $\,15,\,30,\,45,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(10,15)=30.$

To find the $\text{LCM}$ of $(y+1)^{6}$ and $(y+1)^{4},$ we raise $(y+1)$ to the largest power that appears in the expressions, which is $6.$ Therefore,

$$
\text{LCM}((y+1)^{6},\,(y+1)^{4})=(y+1)^{6}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\text{LCM}(10(y+1)^{6},\,15(y+1)^{4})=30\cdot (y+1)^{6}=30(y+1)^{6}.
$$

after.problem: Find the least common multiple of the polynomials $4(z+2)^{2}(w-5)^{2}$ and $7(z+2)^{3}(w-5)^{4}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(4,7):$

- Multiples of $4:$ $\,4,\,8,\,12,\,16,\,20,\,24,\,28,\,32,…$

- Multiples of $7:$ $\,7,\,14,\,21,\,28,\,35,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(4,7)=28.$

To find the $\text{LCM}$ of $(z+2)^{2}(w-5)^{2}$ and $(z+2)^{3}(w-5)^{4},$ we find the largest powers for $(z+2)$ and $(w-5)$ that appear in the expressions:

- For $(z+2)^{2}$ and $(z+2)^{3},$ the largest power is $3.$

- For $(w-5)^{2}$ and $(w-5)^{4},$ the largest power is $4.$

Now, we raise $(z+2)$ and $(w-5)$ to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

$$
\text{LCM}((z+2)^{2}(w-5)^{2},\,(z+2)^{3}(w-5)^{4})=(z+2)^{3}\cdot (w-5)^{4}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\text{LCM}(4(z+2)^{2}(w-5)^{2},\,7(z+2)^{3}(w-5)^{4})=28(z+2)^{3}(w-5)^{4}.
$$

Find the least common multiple of the polynomials 4(z+2)2(w−5)2 and 7(z+2)3(w−5)4.

a
 28(z+2)3(w−5)4
b
42(z+2)2(w−5)5
c
28(z+2)4(w−5)6
d
 28(z+2)2(w−5)4
e
 42(z+2)2(w−5)4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the least common multiple (LCM) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find LCM(4,7):

  • Multiples of 4: 4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,…

  • Multiples of 7: 7,14,21,28,35,…

So, LCM(4,7)=28.

To find the LCM of (z+2)2(w−5)2 and (z+2)3(w−5)4, we find the largest powers for (z+2) and (w−5) that appear in the expressions:

  • For (z+2)2 and (z+2)3, the largest power is 3.

  • For (w−5)2 and (w−5)4, the largest power is 4.

Now, we raise (z+2) and (w−5) to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

LCM((z+2)2(w−5)2,(z+2)3(w−5)4)=(z+2)3⋅(w−5)4.

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

LCM(4(z+2)2(w−5)2,7(z+2)3(w−5)4)=28(z+2)3(w−5)4.

after.problem: Find the least common multiple of the polynomials $20{x}^{7}(y+2),$ $\,10{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},$ and $12{x}^{4}(y+2)^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of three polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(20,10,12):$

- Multiples of $20:$ $\,20,\,40,\,60,\,80,\,100,\,…$

- Multiples of $10:$ $\,10,\,20,\,30,\,40,\,50,\,60,\,70,\,…$

- Multiples of $12:$ $\,12,\,24,\,36,\,48,\,60,\,72,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(20,10,12)=60.$

To find the $\text{LCM}$ of ${x}^{7}(y+2),{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},$ and ${x}^{4}(y+2)^{2},$ we find the largest powers for $x$ and $(y+2)$ that appear in all these expressions:

- For ${x}^{7},\,{x}^{6},$ and ${x}^{4},$ the largest power is $7.$

- For $(y+2),(y+2)^{3},$ and $(y+2)^{2},$ the largest power is $3.$

Now, we raise $x$ and $(y+2)$ to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

$$
\text{LCM}({x}^{7}(y+2),\,{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},\,{x}^{4}(y+2)^{2})={x}^{7}\cdot (y+2)^{3}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{LCM}(20{x}^{7}(y+2),\,10{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},\,12{x}^{4}(y+2)^{2}) & = \\ 60\cdot {x}^{7}\cdot (y+2)^{3} & = \\ 60{x}^{7}(y+2)^{3} & .\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the least common multiple (LCM) of three polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find LCM(20,10,12):

  • Multiples of 20: 20,40,60,80,100,…

  • Multiples of 10: 10,20,30,40,50,60,70,…

  • Multiples of 12: 12,24,36,48,60,72,…

So, LCM(20,10,12)=60.

To find the LCM of x7(y+2),x6(y+2)3, and x4(y+2)2, we find the largest powers for x and (y+2) that appear in all these expressions:

  • For x7,x6, and x4, the largest power is 7.

  • For (y+2),(y+2)3, and (y+2)2, the largest power is 3.

Now, we raise x and (y+2) to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

LCM(x7(y+2),x6(y+2)3,x4(y+2)2)=x7⋅(y+2)3.

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

LCM(20x7(y+2),10x6(y+2)3,12x4(y+2)2)=60⋅x7⋅(y+2)3=60x7(y+2)3.
